Private-pay prices for 4–16 bed homes. CareScout's $7,173 Maryland median is for a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S47]; the $6,100 small-home price is an operator assumption.

sections.executive_summary:
Maryland calls assisted living an **Assisted Living Program (ALP)**. It is licensed by the Maryland Department of Health's **Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ)** under Health-General §19-1801 et seq. and **COMAR 10.07.14**, which was rewritten effective **April 28, 2025** [S31][S1][S25]. Each license names a bed count and one of three levels of care: **Level 1 (low), Level 2 (moderate) or Level 3 (high)** [S67][S2]. The same license covers a 4-bed house and a 150-unit community.

**The market is made of small homes.** OHCQ counted **1,699 programs with 25,391 beds**; **1,507 (89%) had 16 or fewer beds** and **897 had 6 or fewer** [S32]. A 2024 legislative note put 77% of programs at 9 or fewer beds [S29]. OHCQ reported **1,617 licensed programs in February 2026** [S33]. Small homes cluster in Baltimore City (395 of 402 programs at 16 beds or fewer) and Prince George's County (294 of 304) [S32].

**There is no OHCQ application fee**, but two people requirements have tightened. From **July 1, 2026, every assisted living manager must hold a license** from the Board of Long-Term Care Administrators ($100 application + $200 license) [S28][S29]. The manager must also complete an **80-hour approved course with an exam**, plus 20 hours of CE every two years [S30][S6]. Every program also needs a **delegating nurse**: an RN under contract who has taken the Board of Nursing course and observes every resident on site **at least every 45 days** [S9].

**Revenue is mostly private pay.** CareScout's 2025 Maryland median is **$7,173/month** for a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S47]. Medicaid pays through the **Home and Community-Based Options Waiver (Community Options, or CO, Waiver)** at **$90.74/day (Level II) or $114.51/day (Level III)** for services only [S34][S38]. The resident may be charged no more than **$420/month for room and board** [S36]. Demand for waiver beds is large: **23,461 people were on the CO Waiver registry** in June 2025 [S41].

**Bottom line from the P&L.** At 90% occupancy, a 4-bed home loses money because one paid caregiver must be present around the clock. An 8-bed home roughly breaks even. A **16-bed Level 3 home is clearly profitable** (about +$27,600/month), and stays below the 17-bed line where extra building and food-service rules start. A 40-bed facility is the most profitable but needs far more capital. Each waiver resident brings in about $3,900/month, compared with $6,100 for a modeled private-pay resident. Waiver beds work as a minority share in a 16-bed home, but not in an 8-bed home. See Section 8.
sections.service_model:
### Who is served
An assisted living program provides housing and supportive services, supervision, personalized help, and health-related services to people who need help with daily activities [S31]. Programs may not admit anyone who, at admission, would need more than intermittent nursing care, stage 3–4 wound care, ventilator care, or skilled monitoring of an unstable condition. The exception is a resident whose needs are met through a licensed hospice [S20].

### Levels of care (COMAR 10.07.14.05)
The applicant picks one level and must show staff able to deliver it [S2]:
- **Level 1 (low):** occasional supervision, set-up or reminders with two or more ADLs; help taking medication; occasional, uncomplicated behavior support.
- **Level 2 (moderate):** substantial help with two or more ADLs, or minimal help with any number; may administer medication and monitor effects; frequent behaviors.
- **Level 3 (high):** comprehensive help with any number of ADL deficits; complex medication regimens; nursing overview; chronic behaviors needing intensive supervision.

A program may serve its licensed level and any lower level. Serving a resident above the level needs a written resident-specific waiver from OHCQ [S67]. **CO Waiver assisted living rates exist only for Level II and Level III** [S34]. Confirm with MDH OLTSS whether a Level 1-licensed program can enroll. The model assumes Level 3, which most operators choose so residents can age in place.

### Regulatory framework
- **OHCQ** licenses and surveys programs at least once a year. OHCQ can stretch the interval to 18 months for a clean program [S12].
- **Board of Long-Term Care Administrators** licenses assisted living managers (ALMs) from July 1, 2026 [S28].
- **Board of Nursing** certifies medication technicians (CMTs) and approves the delegating nurse course [S58][S59].
- **Maryland Medicaid (Office of Long Term Services and Supports)** enrolls CO Waiver providers and sets rates [S45].
- An **Alzheimer's Special Care Unit** needs OHCQ's written approval of a disclosure form before it opens, and always needs awake overnight staff [S23][S4][S26].

### Physical standards that shape small homes
- No more than **two residents per room**, with at least **80 sq ft (single)** or **120 sq ft (double)** of functional space [S15].
- At least **one toilet and one sink per 4 occupants**, and one tub or shower per 8 [S16].
- At least **35 sq ft of common space per licensed bed** [S17].
- Hot water blended to **100–120°F** at fixtures [S24].
- Compliance with **NFPA 101**, including Chapter 24 for one- and two-family dwellings [S14].

**At 17 or more beds**, the program also needs:
- corridor assist rails and public restrooms;
- COMAR 10.15.03 food-service compliance and a food service permit;
- a State Engineer site-plan review [S17][S26].

An emergency generator is required only at **50 or more residents** [S14].
sections.licensing_pathway:
OHCQ licensing has **three steps**, set out on the April 2026 application [S26]. **There is no fee to apply** [S26].

**Before you apply**
1. Form a Maryland entity with SDAT: $100 for LLC articles; $20 certificate of status [S54]. OHCQ requires an official letter of good standing [S26].
2. Secure the building by deed or lease (OHCQ must see proof of control) [S3]. If it is in an HOA, condominium or co-op, get the community's written approval [S26].
3. Confirm zoning or use-and-occupancy with the county or city [S3][S26].
4. Hire or become a **licensed ALM**. Required from July 1, 2026: $100 application + $200 license fee, State and FBI criminal history check, about 10 business days after a complete file [S28]. The ALM needs an **80-hour course with exam** (one approved vendor charges $1,209) [S30][S60]. A **Level 3** ALM also needs a 4-year degree, or 2 years of health care experience plus ALM experience or the 80-hour course [S5]. Name an **alternate ALM**: age 21+, with 2 years of health experience [S21].
5. Sign a **delegating nurse** agreement with an RN who completed the Board of Nursing course (e.g., a 16-hour, $298 course) [S9][S59].

**Step One — application and attachments.** Submit the typed application online through OHCQ's "Submit a License Application" link [S26]. Include:
- proof of control of the building;
- HOA approval, if applicable;
- **a business plan and a 1-year operating budget**;
- the SDAT good-standing letter;
- the Alzheimer's unit disclosure form, if applicable [S26][S3].

Do not start Step Two until OHCQ says Step One is complete [S26].

**Step Two — additional documents** [S26]:
- **Site plan.** Under 17 beds, a scaled sketch is enough. 17+ beds need an approved State Engineer plan review (667-203-9124).
- **Use and occupancy permit** or zoning approval.
- **Fire inspection report.** In Baltimore City and Baltimore County, programs of 1–16 beds submit the local health department environmental report instead.
- **Food service permit** (17+ beds only).
- **Uniform Disclosure Statement** and resident agreement.
- **Workers' compensation** declaration page, or a certificate of compliance/exemption.

**Step Three — on-site survey** [S26]. The surveyor tours the building, interviews staff and reviews:
- background checks for owners, managers, staff and household members;
- ALM, alternate ALM and delegating nurse credentials;
- 12 required policies (e.g., abuse, emergency plan, quality assurance, complaints);
- a **4-week menu reviewed by a licensed dietitian or nutritionist** [S26][S18].

If deficiencies are cited, you have **10 business days** to submit a plan of correction [S26]. OHCQ may approve unconditionally, approve with conditions (including a required management firm for up to 24 months), or deny [S3]. It may also issue a **provisional license** while non-hazardous deficiencies are corrected [S3]. **You may not operate until a license or provisional license is issued** [S3]. An incomplete application may be closed after **180 days** [S3]. OHCQ publishes no processing time.

**After licensure**
- Post the license in a common area [S67].
- Stay in good standing with SDAT. OHCQ may void the license 60 days after notice of non-compliance [S13].
- Report building, fire or sanitary code citations to OHCQ within 7 days [S13].
- Give **60 days' notice** (49 or fewer beds) before a change of ownership, relocation or closure [S13].

sections.reimbursement:
### 1. Private pay (the main payer)
Most Maryland residents pay privately. CareScout's 2025 median is **$7,173/month** ($86,070/year), compared with $6,200 nationally [S47]. That figure is for a **private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community**. Shared rooms in small homes usually sell for less, so the model prices 4–16 bed homes at **$6,100/month**. That price is an operator assumption about 15% below the median; set yours from local comparables. Rate increases need **45 days' written notice** in the resident agreement unless a change in the resident's medical condition requires it (COMAR 10.07.14.27A(2)(e)) [S73].

### 2. Medicaid: Home and Community-Based Options Waiver (CO Waiver)
Maryland Medicaid pays assisted living under a **1915(c) waiver**, fee-for-service. It is not paid through HealthChoice managed care.

**Who qualifies.** Participants must:
- be 18 or older and need a **nursing facility level of care**;
- have income no higher than **300% of the SSI benefit** (300% × $994 = $2,982/month in 2026) and assets of no more than $2,000–$2,500 [S45][S36][S62].

**How you get paid.**
- Medicaid pays a **daily service rate**: **W0226 Level II $90.74; W0227 Level III $114.51**. Lower W0228/W0229 rates apply on medical day care days [S34].
- Rates are effective **July 1, 2024**. No later rate transmittal exists. MDH kept FY2026 LTSS rates unchanged [S72], the FY2027 budget holds LTSS rates level [S40], and the FY2026 case-management rate matches FY2025 [S42]. Confirm with MDH before billing.
- Waiver payments **exclude room and board** [S38]. The resident pays room and board, **capped at $420/month** [S36]. The resident keeps a personal needs allowance.
- Any income left over is the resident's "cost of care." The resident pays it **directly to you**, and Medicaid reduces its payment by the same amount [S36]. Your total is therefore about **$114.51 × 30.42 + $420 ≈ $3,903/month** at Level III, or about **$3,180** at Level II.
- Medicaid pays the lesser of your customary charge or the rate [S35].
- Since **October 1, 2026**, assisted living claims go through **LTSSMaryland**, not eMedicaid. The billing week runs Thursday–Wednesday, with weekly direct deposit [S43].

**Extra provider rules for waiver beds** [S37]:
- at least **1 staff per 8 residents during daytime hours**;
- a manager who is a physician, RN, LPN, or has 3 years of direct-care experience;
- an alternate manager;
- quarterly case-manager visits, and notice to the case manager within 1 working day of a significant change.

You may limit waiver residents to approved designated units [S37]. Bed-hold charges may not exceed the waiver per diem [S37].

### 3. Senior Assisted Living Subsidy (SALS)
The Maryland Department of Aging subsidy pays **up to $1,056/month** directly to the provider. It covers residents aged 62+ with income at or below 60% of the State median, and assets up to $19,000 (single). The facility must have a service agreement with the local Area Agency on Aging [S46]. SALS can make a moderate-income resident affordable without the waiver's $420 room-and-board limit.

### 4. Other payers
Long-term care insurance and VA Aid & Attendance pay residents, not providers. Medicare does not pay for assisted living.
sections.operations:
### Staffing rules (COMAR 10.07.14.14)
The rule sets **no numeric ratio** [S4]. Instead, the program must:
- write a staffing plan based on residents' needs, with enough staff for scheduled and unscheduled needs 24 hours a day;
- have **a staff member present whenever a resident is in the building**, or is expected back;
- provide **awake overnight staff** when a resident's Resident Assessment Tool triggers it. OHCQ may waive this for an approved electronic monitoring system, but never on an Alzheimer's unit;
- keep a dated staffing schedule on site for 18 months [S4].

CO Waiver homes must also keep **1 staff per 8 residents in daytime** [S37]. Every model in Section 8 staffs one person awake 24/7, which also covers the awake-overnight triggers.

### Required roles
- **Licensed ALM** (on site or on call), plus an **alternate ALM** [S5][S21][S28].
- **Delegating nurse (RN)** [S9]:
  - signed agreement, and completion of the Board of Nursing course;
  - on site to observe each resident **at least every 45 days**;
  - on call at all times (or a qualified alternate);
  - issues nursing orders and reviews the ALM's assessments.
- **ALM and delegating nurse meet every 6 months** to review resident changes and pharmacy findings [S22].
- **Medication technicians.** Unlicensed staff who administer medications must finish the Board of Nursing **20-hour CMT course** and be certified [S10][S58][S65]. CMTs renew every 2 years, with 100 practice hours and a 4-hour clinical update [S58].
- **Pharmacist review** at least every 6 months for any resident on **9 or more medications** [S10].
- **On-site nursing** is required only when the delegating nurse or a practitioner orders it [S4].

### Staff qualifications and training (COMAR 10.07.14.19) [S8]
- **Age:** direct-care staff must be 18+ (16–17 only if a CNA or in CNA training).
- **Health:** TB screening and MMR/varicella immunity.
- **Background check** completed within 30 days before hire.
- **Annual training** in fire and life safety, infection control, food safety and disaster plans.
- **First aid** every 2 years; enough CPR-trained staff for 24-hour coverage.
- **6 hours of cognitive impairment / mental health / behavioral training** within 120 days for personal-care staff (2 hours for others), then 2 hours (or 1 hour) every year.
- Non-CNA personal-care staff must show competence to the delegating nurse. They may work up to 10 days accompanied while doing so.

### Resident processes
- **Before admission:** complete the Resident Assessment Tool within 30 days before admission [S11].
- **Service plan:** write it within 30 days of admission; review assessments and plans every 6 months [S11][S1].
- **Meals:** three meals and snacks daily from a dietitian-reviewed 4-week menu. Re-review every 3 years [S18].
- **Resident funds:** if you manage residents' money, carry a bond, letter of credit or net assets equal to the average monthly balance [S19].

### Systems
- Maryland has no EVV requirement for assisted living.
- **Waiver billing runs through LTSSMaryland** (helpdesk 1-855-463-5877) [S43].
- **Medicaid enrollment moved to MPRIME on October 13, 2026.** An SDAT number in good standing is mandatory [S44].
- An eMAR system is an operator choice, budgeted in the P&L.
sections.market_conditions:
**Supply.** Licensed program counts went from 1,369 in FY2011 to 1,672 in FY2021 [S32]; 1,721 were reported in June 2023 [S29] and 1,617 in February 2026 [S33]. Between FY2011 and FY2021, OHCQ recorded 33–252 closures and 109–218 initial surveys a year [S32]. Turnover is high, so new homes keep entering and leaving.

**Pricing.**
- CareScout 2025 puts Maryland assisted living at **$7,173/month**, 16% above the U.S. median of $6,200 [S47].
- The CO Waiver Level III service rate of $114.51/day plus $420 room and board totals about **$3,903/month**, or 54% of the private median [S34][S36].
- SALS can add up to $1,056/month for moderate-income seniors [S46].

**Wages (BLS May 2025, Maryland) [S49][S50]:**

| Role | Median hourly |
|---|---|
| Home health & personal care aides | $18.29 |
| Nursing assistants (CMT proxy) | $20.79 |
| Registered nurses | $47.98 |
| LPNs | $35.89 |
| Cooks, institution | $19.89 |
| Housekeepers | $17.07 |

Manager pay benchmarks: medical and health services managers, 10th percentile $77,560 and 25th $101,200; social and community service managers, 10th percentile $58,050 and 25th $71,720 [S49].

The **State minimum wage is $15.00**. **Montgomery County** requires $18.00 for employers with 51+ workers, $16.50 for 11–50 and $15.95 for 10 or fewer, and **Howard County** $16.00, all as of July 1, 2026 [S51]. Every modeled direct-care wage ($18.29–$20.79) is above all of these. Montgomery rates rise each July with CPI [S51].

**Rent.** HUD FY2027 Small Area FMRs for a 4-bedroom home:
- **$2,750** in Parkville (Baltimore County) [S56];
- **$4,050** in Upper Marlboro (Prince George's) [S57].

DC-suburb homes cost about 47% more to lease.

**Policy trends.**
- Rewritten rules (April 2025) [S25].
- Manager licensure (July 2026) [S28].
- A 2026 interagency workgroup on unlicensed programs [S33].
- No LTSS rate increase in FY2026 [S72] or FY2027 (level rates) [S40].
sections.financial_narrative:
### How the P&L is built
Revenue per resident × occupied residents, minus staffing (with payroll burden) and operating costs. Default occupancy is 90% [S48]. Ramp-up is an operator planning assumption: 4- and 8-bed homes start at 1 resident and add 1 a month, the 16-bed home adds 2 a month, and the 40-bed facility starts at 4 and adds 3 a month.

**Revenue.**
- Small homes are priced at **$6,100/month**, an operator assumption about 15% below CareScout's $7,173 Maryland median [S47].
- The 40-bed facility uses the full median.
- Waiver residents bring **$114.51 × 30.42 + $420 = $3,903/month** (Level III) [S34][S36].

**Staffing.**
- Every configuration keeps a staff member present 24/7 [S4].
- Medication staff are paid the Maryland nursing-assistant median ($20.79) as a CMT proxy; other aides $18.29 [S49].
- The delegating nurse is modeled at the $47.98 RN median: 3–8 fixed hours a month plus 1.5 hours per resident (operator estimate — verify locally) [S9].
- ALM pay uses Maryland BLS manager percentiles. The 4-bed ALM is half-time.

**Burden.** 8.3% payroll taxes [S53][S66][S52], plus 4% workers' comp and 5% benefits (both estimates).

**Operating costs.**
- **Rent is fixed:** 4 beds $2,750 (HUD) [S56]; 8 beds $4,125; 16 beds $8,000; 40 beds $20,000. The last three are operator estimates.
- **Fixed utility base:** $100 per licensed bed.
- **Per-resident costs:** food, supplies, insurance, pharmacist reviews, repairs and activities.
- **Fixed overhead:** software, accounting, marketing, training and the $300 SDAT annual report [S54]. There is **no OHCQ license fee** [S26].
- **County business personal property tax:** businesses with $20,000+ of furnishings and equipment must file SDAT Form 1 and pay county tax (e.g., Baltimore County $2.75 per $100 of assessed value) [S69][S70]. Modeled at $10 (4 beds), $40 (8 beds), $85 (16 beds) and $230 (40 beds) a month — operator estimate, verify with your county.

### Results at 90% occupancy (monthly, approximate)
| Configuration | Revenue | Staffing + burden | Opex | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4-bed private pay | $21,960 | $21,110 | $6,680 | about –$5,800 |
| 8-bed private pay | $43,920 | $29,530 | $10,810 | about +$3,600 |
| 8-bed, 3 waiver residents | $37,990 | $29,530 | $10,810 | about –$2,300 |
| 16-bed private pay | $87,840 | $39,520 | $20,720 | about +$27,600 |
| 16-bed, 25% waiver | $79,930 | $39,520 | $20,720 | about +$19,700 |
| 40-bed private pay | $258,230 | $97,590 | $51,550 | about +$109,100 |

### Key drivers and sensitivity
- **Size.** 24-hour presence costs about $17,800/month including burden at any size. Spread over 3.6 residents (4 beds) it sinks the model; over 14.4 residents (16 beds) it is affordable.
  - At 90% occupancy the 4-bed home needs **about $7,700/month** per resident to break even with a half-time paid ALM.
  - With the **owner as ALM** it needs about $6,900; the loss at $6,100 shrinks to about –$3,000.
  - An owner-ALM lifts the 8-bed home to about +$9,300 (break-even about $4,800/month at 90% occupancy, versus about $5,600 with a paid ALM).
- **Private-pay price.** At $5,500/month the 16-bed home earns about +$19,000 and the 8-bed home about –$700. At the $7,173 median the 16-bed home earns about +$43,000.
- **Waiver share.** Each waiver resident brings about $2,200/month less than a $6,100 private-pay resident. In the 16-bed home, full cost per resident is about $4,180, so waiver beds are below full cost but well above the roughly $730 a month of variable cost per resident. They help fill empty beds but cannot carry a home alone.
- **Wages.** Adding $2/hour to every aide and CMT (e.g., a tight local labor market) cuts the 16-bed result to about +$24,700 and the 8-bed result to about +$1,300.

The generator calculates break-even from these inputs.
sections.risks:
- **Medicaid rates are flat.** CO Waiver assisted living rates have not risen since July 1, 2024, MDH kept FY2026 LTSS rates unchanged [S72], and the FY2027 budget holds them level [S34][S40]. DLS recommended cutting HCBS rates 2% in FY2026 [S39]. Wages keep rising, so waiver margins shrink each year.
- **Room-and-board cap.** Waiver residents can be charged only up to $420/month for room and board [S36], far below the cost of housing and food. Confirm the current figure with MDH.
- **Waiver enrollment delays.** 23,461 people are on the registry and a third of authorized slots went unfilled in FY2025 [S41]. A resident you accept may wait months for waiver approval.
- **People licensure.** From July 1, 2026, running a program without a licensed ALM exposes you to Board action. Losing your ALM means an interim provisional license lasting at most 90 days, extendable by 30 for good cause (Health Occ. §9-3A-01(b)(2)) [S71]. Failing to employ a qualified ALM can bring a civil money penalty up to $10,000 [S6].
- **Delegating nurse dependency.** If the RN contract ends, the program must notify OHCQ and still cover the 45-day visits [S9][S5]. Contract RN rates often exceed the BLS median used here.
- **Small-home economics.** Homes of 4–8 beds depend on owner labor and high occupancy. Two vacancies in an 8-bed home erase its profit.
- **Survey and enforcement.** OHCQ surveys every 12–18 months [S12]. The most-cited deficiency in FY2021 was staff qualifications [S32]. A suspension or revocation bars owners and managers from another license for 10 years [S3].
- **Local costs.** Montgomery County minimum wages rise each July [S51]. DC-suburb rents run about 47% above Baltimore County [S56][S57]. Local fire authorities may require sprinklers or other upgrades [S14].
- **Billing transitions.** Waiver billing moved to LTSSMaryland on Oct. 1, 2026 [S43], and enrollment moved to MPRIME on Oct. 13, 2026. Any lapse in SDAT good standing now suspends Medicaid payments automatically [S44].
sections.recommendations:
1. **Size for 16 beds if you can.** At 9–16 beds the 24-hour staffing cost is spread across enough residents to profit. Staying at 16 avoids the 17-bed requirements: State Engineer plan review, food service permit, public restrooms and assist rails [S17][S26]. The 16-bed private-pay model earns about +$27,600/month at 90% occupancy.
2. **If you start with 4–8 beds, plan to work in the home.** Serve as the licensed ALM yourself, and cover shifts or live in. With you as the ALM, break-even at 90% occupancy is about $6,900/month (4 beds) and about $4,800/month (8 beds); with a paid ALM it is about $7,700 (4 beds) and about $5,600 (8 beds). Price above those levels, and add a second home later.
3. **License at Level 3.** It lets residents age in place, and it is required to bill the waiver's higher rate ($114.51/day) [S2][S34].
4. **Get the people requirements done first.**
   - Enroll the ALM in an approved 80-hour course and apply for the Board license ($300) [S60][S28].
   - Sign a delegating nurse agreement [S9].
   - Put every medication-passing staff member through the 20-hour CMT course [S58].
5. **Use the CO Waiver for a minority of beds** (about 25% in a 16-bed home). Enroll in MPRIME after licensure [S44], and set up LTSSMaryland billing [S43]. Build referrals with case managers and nursing-home discharge planners, since nursing-home residents can skip the registry [S45]. For moderate-income seniors, sign an AAA service agreement to accept **SALS** (up to $1,056/month) [S46].
6. **Budget conservatively.** Use local private-pay comparables rather than the $7,173 community median [S47]. Use your county's actual rent [S56][S57]. Carry a working-capital reserve for the ramp-up and send OHCQ the required 1-year budget [S3].
7. **Build survey readiness into operations.** Keep the 12 required policies, staff training proof, 45-day RN notes, 6-month assessment reviews and pharmacist reviews current [S26][S8][S9][S10][S11]. The goal is clean surveys and the 18-month survey interval [S12].

occupancy.rationale: NIC MAP reports assisted living occupancy of 88.4% across the 31 primary U.S. markets in 2Q 2026 [S48]. corrections_vs_previous: The old checklist told applicants to pay an annual OHCQ license fee of $50 (1–4 beds), $100 (5–15) or $200 (16+). The current OHCQ application states 'There is no fee to apply for a license' [S26], and the April 2025 rule has no fee section. The old figures do not even match the 2016 table ($50/$75/$125… per year) [S63].

The old checklist did not mention that, since July 1, 2026, every assisted living manager must be licensed by the Board of Long-Term Care Administrators ($100 + $200) [S28], or that the 80-hour course and exam now apply regardless of home size [S30][S6].

The old checklist omitted the delegating nurse (mandatory RN agreement, Board of Nursing course, 45-day on-site visits) [S9] and the CMT requirement for staff who give medications [S10]. These are two of the largest recurring compliance costs.

The old checklist said a '$50,000 surety bond' is required if handling resident funds. The rule requires a bond, letter of credit or net assets equal to the average monthly balance of resident funds held [S19].

Many old citations pointed to the wrong COMAR sections. For example, .21 (Delegating Nurse) was cited for zoning and physical plant; .09 (Licensure Standards Waiver) for background checks; .27 for Alzheimer's units (correct: .32); and 42 CFR §483.40, a nursing-home rule [S1].

The old checklist had applicants get the fire inspection and zoning approval before submitting the application. OHCQ's three-step process asks for those in Step Two, after OHCQ reviews Step One [S26].

The old checklist said OHCQ requires general liability insurance with a $1M minimum and OHCQ as certificate holder. COMAR 10.07.14 sets no liability-insurance requirement; only workers' compensation proof is required [S26][S3].
The old checklist promised 8–10 weeks of processing and a 'Montgomery County $60/bed' local fee. No source supports either figure; OHCQ publishes no processing time [S3].
